content: The World Health Organization (WHO) has published its 2021 consolidated guidelines on tuberculosis (TB) diagnosis, specifically focusing on rapid diagnostic methods for TB detection. These guidelines, referred to as Module 3: Diagnosis, provide updated recommendations and methodologies for the use of rapid diagnostic tools to detect TB and drug-resistant TB (DR-TB). The guidelines are available in both electronic and print formats, with ISBNs 978-92-4-002941-5 and 978-92-4-002942-2, respectively. The publication is distributed under a Creative Commons license, allowing users to copy, redistribute, and adapt the content for non-commercial purposes, provided proper citation is given. However, the use of the WHO logo is prohibited, and any adaptations must be licensed under the same or an equivalent Creative Commons license. Translations of the document must include a disclaimer stating that WHO is not responsible for the accuracy or content of the translation, and the original English version remains the authoritative edition. The guidelines were developed through a collaborative effort involving multiple professionals and organizations. Separate Guideline Development Groups (GDGs) were established for each section of the guidelines, ensuring a comprehensive and multidisciplinary approach. The recommendations are based on systematic reviews, meta-analyses, and expert consensus. The document includes detailed sections on various diagnostic tools and methods, such as low-complexity automated nucleic acid amplification tests (NAATs) for detecting resistance to isoniazid and second-line anti-TB agents, first-line and second-line line probe assays (LPAs), and high-complexity reverse hybridization-based NAATs for detecting pyrazinamide resistance. It also provides systematic reviews and meta-analyses on the diagnostic accuracy of these tools. Acknowledgments are given to the numerous contributors, including members of the GDGs, external review groups, systematic review teams, and technical consultants. These individuals represent a wide range of expertise and institutions from around the world, including national TB programs, academic institutions, research organizations, and civil society groups. The guidelines were developed under the oversight of the WHO Global TB Programme, with input from the WHO Global HIV Programme and other relevant departments. Funding for the development of these guidelines was provided by the United States Agency for International Development (USAID) and the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation. The funding agencies had no influence on the content or recommendations of the guidelines. The publication emphasizes the importance of rapid and accurate diagnostic tools in the fight against TB and DR-TB, highlighting the need for continued research, collaboration, and innovation in this field. It serves as a critical resource for healthcare providers, policymakers, and researchers working to improve TB diagnosis and treatment outcomes globally.
